title: Windows Fundamentals I: the system you will audit
description: Editions and architecture, the Registry, UAC and management tools.

1.title: Editions, architecture and the C: drive
1.body:
## One ecosystem, many editions

**Home** (consumer), **Pro** (domain + BitLocker + Remote Desktop), **Enterprise**
(full GPOs, corporate) and **Server** (the domain controllers you'll attack
in Active Directory). The edition determines which attack/abuse techniques exist.

## The file system: NTFS and its key folders

| Path | What's there |
|---|---|
| `C:\Windows` | the system (System32 = critical binaries) |
| `C:\Program Files` | 64-bit software |
| `C:\Program Files (x86)` | 32-bit software |
| `C:\Users\<usuario>` | profiles (Documents, Desktop, NTUSER.DAT…) |
| `C:\ProgramData` | application data (hidden, writable by users) |

NTFS brings **granular ACLs** (richer than rwx), **alternate data streams (ADS)** to
hide data (`archivo.txt:oculto`) and **journaling**. In AD you'll also see mapped network
drives and shared resources (`\\servidor\recurso`).

Management tools you should already recognize: **Control Panel**, **Computer
Management** (local users, services, Event Viewer) and **msconfig/taskmgr**
for processes and startup.

2.title: The Registry: the system's database
2.body:
## Five hives that will rule your enumeration

```text
HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT   (HKCR)  file associations
HKEY_CURRENT_USER   (HKCU)  current user's configuration
HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE  (HKLM)  configuration of the WHOLE machine  ← the gold mine
HKEY_USERS          (HKU)   all loaded profiles
HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG         current hardware profile
```

Open the editor with **regedit** (or from a terminal: `reg query ...`). Paths you'll
memorize forever:

```powershell
# Autostart (classic persistence):
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

# Exact system version (enumeration):
HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion
```

Every installed program leaves a trace in `HKLM\SOFTWARE`. Every portable program
(one that runs without being installed) also leaves one in `HKCU\SOFTWARE`. The
Registry is the fastest way to answer: WHAT is installed, WHAT starts on its own and
WHICH exact version of Windows is it?

windows-fundamentos-1-t02-q01.hint: regedit. That one, exactly as written.

3.title: UAC, sessions and the 'Run as administrator' button
3.body:
## UAC: the nightclub bouncer

**UAC** (User Account Control) separates two security tokens:

- **Filtered token**: your normal session — no access to critical areas of the system.
- **Elevated token**: when you click "Yes" on the UAC prompt — access to `C:\Windows`,
  `HKLM`, taking ownership of files, opening low ports…

A normal process run by an Administrator user does NOT have the elevated token by default:
that's why a malicious binary with normal privileges can't, for example, write
to `C:\Windows\System32`. **UAC bypasses** = techniques that trick trusted
auto-elevating processes into handing over the full token.

## Special accounts you should know

- **Administrator**: the all-powerful local account (sometimes disabled).
- **SYSTEM (LocalSystem)**: the context of system services — MORE powerful
  than Administrator in certain internal respects.
- **Guest**: limited access, almost always disabled.

When you compromise a Windows machine, your typical goal is: normal user →
UAC bypass → Administrator → migration to SYSTEM → credential theft →
Active Directory. That complete path is practiced in the path's AD module.

windows-fundamentos-1-t03-q01.prompt: What is the mechanism called that asks for confirmation (and elevates privileges) when a program needs administrator permissions?

windows-fundamentos-1-t03-q02.prompt: What privileges does a process launched 'as administrator' have compared with a normal one?

options.a: The same: only the icon changes
options.b: Full access to HKLM, system files and taking ownership of processes
options.c: It can only change the wallpaper

windows-fundamentos-1-t03-q03.prompt: Which built-in Windows account has ALL privileges (more than Administrator)?
windows-fundamentos-1-t03-q03.hint: The one that doesn't even show up in the user list.
